reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO nutrition guidance
clinicalPearls: Produces a macrocytic megaloblastic anaemia indistinguishable on the blood film from vitamin B12 deficiency
Body stores are small, so deficiency can develop within months of poor intake, unlike B12
Common precipitants include poor diet, chronic alcohol use, malabsorption, and states of increased demand such as pregnancy, lactation, and haemolysis
Adequate periconceptional folate reduces the risk of fetal neural tube defects, underpinning supplementation and food fortification programmes
Certain drugs interfere with folate metabolism, including some antiepileptics and antifolate agents
Unlike B12 deficiency, isolated folate deficiency does not typically cause the myelopathy of subacute combined degeneration
B12 status should be checked before folate replacement because giving folate alone in a B12-deficient patient can worsen neurological disease
reference.pathophysiology: Folate provides one-carbon units essential for purine and thymidylate synthesis and for methylation reactions, working closely with vitamin B12 in homocysteine remethylation. Deficiency impairs DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells, producing megaloblastic haematopoiesis and ineffective erythropoiesis. Because hepatic and body stores are limited, negative balance from inadequate intake, malabsorption, excess loss, or increased requirement rapidly leads to deficiency. Impaired one-carbon metabolism during embryogenesis is linked to failure of neural tube closure.
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and blood film for megaloblastic changes
Serum and red cell folate, with red cell folate reflecting longer-term status
Concurrent vitamin B12 measurement before starting replacement
Homocysteine, which rises in folate deficiency, when clarification is needed
Assessment for alcohol use, malabsorption, and increased demand states
redFlags: Severe symptomatic anaemia with cardiorespiratory compromise
Deficiency in pregnancy given the risk of neural tube defects
Pancytopenia from severe megaloblastic marrow failure
Unrecognised coexisting B12 deficiency at risk of neurological harm from folate-only treatment
reference.prognosis: Deficiency responds promptly and completely to replacement and correction of the underlying cause; the main lasting harm relates to fetal effects when deficiency occurs in early pregnancy.
pitfalls: Replacing folate without excluding B12 deficiency
Overlooking chronic alcohol use as both a cause and a barrier to recovery
Assuming a normal serum folate excludes deficiency when recent intake has temporarily corrected it
Missing an underlying malabsorptive disorder such as coeliac disease
management: Replace folate with oral folic acid, continued until the deficiency is corrected and any ongoing cause is resolved
Measure and correct any coexisting vitamin B12 deficiency before or alongside folate replacement, since folate alone can precipitate or worsen the neurological damage of B12 deficiency
Identify and treat the underlying cause — improve dietary intake, address chronic alcohol use, and investigate malabsorption such as coeliac disease
Review and adjust drugs that impair folate metabolism, including certain antiepileptics and antifolates such as methotrexate, for which folinic acid rescue is used
Advise periconceptional and first-trimester folic acid supplementation to reduce the risk of foetal neural tube defects, at higher dose where risk is increased
Monitor the haematological response with a rising reticulocyte count and normalising full blood count
